chunks: From him, from Ayoub ibn Nuhr, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darradj, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a property (ضيعة), and he used to enter it and exit from it. When he paid the money, he went to the property, inspected it thoroughly, then returned and asked the seller to take back the deal (istaqala), but the seller did not agree. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If he had inspected it or looked at ninety-nine pieces of it, and one piece remained that he had not seen, he would have the option of inspection (khiyar al-ru'yah) regarding that.'

key_terms.اسْتَقَالَ: Asked for the option of cancellation / rescission.
key_terms.خِيَارُ الرُّؤْيَةِ: The option of inspection, a right allowing the buyer to cancel the contract if the item differs from what was seen or if not all parts were inspected.
key_terms.ضَيْعَةً: A property or estate, often implying agricultural land or a collection of assets.
key_terms.قَلَّبَهَا: Inspected it thoroughly / turned it over.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the buyer's right to cancel a sale if they haven't seen every part of the purchased property?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* to clarify the extent of the buyer's right of inspection (*khiyar al-ru'yah*) in property transactions. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the option remains valid as long as even a single part of the multi-part asset remains unseen, emphasizing that the right is not extinguished by the inspection of the majority (ninety-nine parts). This principle underscores the Shia legal emphasis on transparency and the buyer's right to verify the entirety of the subject matter before finalizing the contract.
